extmeta.ImageDescription:
A fragment of a medieval tile. The tile is bi chrome and unglazed dating to 1250-1500 AD, but likely to be 1250-1350. The fragment is a sub triangular shape, and has one of the original corners of the tile. The tile is a pinky red colour, and is decorated with a yellow white slip. The design is a semi circular line across the corner, with a trefoil or triangular shape into the corner. Coming out from the direction of the centre of the tile is a curvilinear line. It is unclear what the tile originally depicted. There is no decoration on the reverse, there are three drilled holes that are 6mm deep. The reverse also has cracks running across it. The tile measures 82.3mm x 72.8mm x 20.00mm, and weighs 15.40g.

Egan 1998, pages 38-40.

extmeta.ImageDescription:
I have indicated the location. You can go and look yourself.

I suspect that a crack: - radiates out from the point of maximum force - tries to minimize it's length - tries to minimize the breaking force

The longest crack is probably the first one.

I have not found a good introduction to the physics of the crack formation. Can anyone help me?

I suspect it is some kind of equilibrium or optimization, the patterns remind me of soap bubble structures.

extmeta.Categories: Barchman Wuytierslaan|Pavements in the Netherlands|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|2012 in Amersfoort
extmeta.ImageDescription:
I'm still fascinated by the cracks in pavement tiles. Just by looking you can see that there are patterns and limitations to the configurations the cracks can take. There are statistical distributions. Notice how sometimes cracks meet at the same place at the edge of a tile. But I have found no article yet on the corresponding physics. These will be quite difficult, I'm sure.

Pavement opposite the train station of Amersfoort.

Am I the only one who has noticed these patterns? Surely not! But I never found anyone writing about them.

extmeta.ImageDescription: While visiting the documenta I could not resist photographing the many tile cracks I saw in Kassel. These German tiles were bigger than the Dutch tiles, I guess 40*40 in stead of 30*30. And the underground is different. Dutch tiles are laid on sand, German tiles are embedded in concrete. And thease light coloured tiles were made from a stone-imitating concrete. I assume they are tougher than the Dutch tiles and that's why they show different crack patterns.
